summary:
Brendan O'Donoghue, a research scientist at Google DeepMind, introduces text diffusion as a forward-looking alternative to standard autoregressive language model generation. The core mechanism mirrors image diffusion: during training, clean token sequences are progressively corrupted with noise, and a neural network learns to fill in the corruption. At inference, the model starts from pure random tokens and iteratively refines the entire canvas over multiple denoising steps, generating the full block simultaneously rather than one token at a time.

A Gemini Diffusion research preview was released approximately one year ago to about 100k users, branching from Gemini 2.0 Flash. Quality was comparable across the board, with slight advantages in code, at much better latencies.

The primary advantage is faster inference due to hardware efficiency. Modern GPUs and TPUs are memory-bandwidth bound. Autoregressive generation streams the entire network per token, whereas text diffusion generates 256 tokens in 24 denoising steps, performing roughly 10x fewer memory transfers. The demo consistently hit about 2,000 raw tokens per second in users' browsers.

Bidirectional attention enables self-correction: in a math problem (answer 39), GPT-4o said 40 and Gemini 2.5 Flash said 42 and never corrected it, while the smaller Gemini Diffusion model guessed 60, then 49, then fixed itself to 39 after completing reasoning. Dynamic computation means more forward passes improve quality roughly monotonically. Adaptive computation lets the model decide when it's finished: 100 digits of pi took 4 steps, FizzBuzz took 18, explaining quantum mechanics took 31. In-place editing allows fixing bugs or adding documentation in the correct location without regenerating all tokens.

Low latency unlocks new applications: a fake Wikipedia with HTML and text generated on the fly, a Reddit clone with AI comments and images, an operating system where every click generates the next screen, and a voice-coded todo app built in 15 seconds.

Q&A revealed further details. Prefill works the same as autoregressive; generation proceeds in fixed-size blocks (e.g., 512, 1000) then continues autoregressively from there, with a vanilla logits prediction head for length. Text diffusion today is discrete diffusion—tokens in, tokens out—though latent-space variants exist in literature. Low-latency diffusion models suit on-device applications (robotics, phones) where batch sizes are small and throughput is not a concern; quality matches frontier models, and the bottleneck is serving throughput, not quality. RL can be applied with algorithmic changes. Initializing from a smaller model's output instead of noise is possible but adds training complexity. Combining diffusion with autoregressive models is also possible.

takeaways: Text diffusion corrupts clean tokens with noise during training and iteratively denoises from pure random tokens at inference, generating entire blocks simultaneously.
Generating 256 tokens in 24 denoising steps requires roughly 10x fewer memory transfers than autoregressive generation, achieving ~2,000 tokens/second.
Bidirectional attention enables self-correction: the smaller Gemini Diffusion model fixed its answer from 60 to 49 to 39, while larger GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Flash made errors they could not fix.
Adaptive computation lets the model self-determine step count: 4 steps for 100 digits of pi, 18 for FizzBuzz, 31 for explaining quantum mechanics.
In-place editing allows targeted fixes—bug fixes, documentation, paragraph insertion—without regenerating all tokens, leveraging surrounding context.
Low latency (~2,000 tokens/sec) unlocks new applications: generated-on-the-fly Wikipedia, Reddit, an AI operating system, and voice-driven live coding.
Lower throughput at large batch sizes is the key disadvantage, making text diffusion expensive to serve at scale but well-suited for on-device, low-batch applications.
Quality matches frontier autoregressive models; the barrier to adoption is serving throughput, not quality.
Text diffusion today is discrete diffusion (tokens in, tokens out); RL and hybrid diffusion-autoregressive approaches are feasible with algorithmic changes.
Initializing from a smaller model instead of noise adds training complexity because the model is trained to expect noise.

sections.title: Introduction to Text Diffusion
sections.summary: O'Donoghue introduces text diffusion by analogy to image/video diffusion: clean tokens are corrupted with noise during training and a neural network learns to denoise; at inference the model starts from pure random tokens and iteratively refines them into coherent text.

sections.title: Gemini Diffusion Research Preview
sections.summary: A Gemini Diffusion research demo was released about one year ago to ~100k users, branching from Gemini 2.0 Flash. Quality was comparable across the board with better latencies, though numbers are now outdated.

sections.title: Difference Between Autoregressive and Diffusion
sections.summary: Autoregressive models generate one token at a time conditioning on previous tokens. Diffusion initializes a long random token canvas and iteratively refines the entire block over multiple passes, attending to future tokens via bidirectional attention.

sections.title: Pros and Cons of Text Diffusion
sections.summary: Advantages: faster inference, bidirectional attention enabling self-correction, adaptive computation, and in-place editing. Main disadvantage: lower throughput at large batch sizes making it expensive to serve at scale, which prevents production deployment.

sections.title: Hardware Efficiency: Why Text Diffusion is Faster
sections.summary: GPUs/TPUs are memory-bandwidth bound; weights and KV cache must stream from HBM to tensor cores. Autoregressive generation streams everything per token, while diffusion generates 256 tokens in 24 steps, doing ~10x fewer memory transfers and achieving near-10x speedup. Gemini Diffusion hit ~2,000 tokens/second in-browser including prefill.

sections.title: Bidirectional Reasoning and Self-Correction
sections.summary: A math problem (answer 39) demonstrates self-correction: after one forward pass the model guessed 60, after two passes it changed to 49, and after three passes it completed reasoning and went back to fix the answer to 39. This bidirectional reasoning and self-correction is a property autoregressive models lack.

sections.title: Comparison with GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Flash
sections.summary: On the same math problem, GPT-4o said 40 and acknowledged its mistake, while Gemini 2.5 Flash said 42 and incorporated the error into its reasoning. Both were much bigger models than Gemini Diffusion, highlighting a fundamental flaw of autoregressive models that diffusion models avoid. Modern reasoning thinking models can mitigate this but punt the problem elsewhere.

sections.title: Dynamic and Adaptive Computation
sections.summary: More forward passes improve quality roughly monotonically across coding evals. Adaptive computation lets the model self-determine when it is finished: 100 digits of pi took 4 steps, FizzBuzz took 18, explaining quantum mechanics took 31. Harder evals like GPQA Diamond took longer; easier ones like MBPP took less time. The model itself decides how much compute to spend.

sections.title: In-place Text Editing
sections.summary: Like image diffusion inpainting, text diffusion can edit specific regions using surrounding context. Demos show bug fixes in code, adding documentation, and inserting a middle paragraph in a story—all done in-place without regenerating all tokens.

sections.title: Low Latency Applications and Demos
sections.summary: Low latency (~2,000 tokens/sec) unlocks new applications: a fake Wikipedia with HTML and text generated on the fly, a Reddit clone with AI comments and images (paired with an image model), an operating system where every click generates the next screen, and a voice-coded todo app built in 15 seconds by an external user.

sections.title: Q&A Session
sections.summary: Q&A covers: same training data is used with algorithmic changes; bigger models tend to require fewer denoising steps; prefill is the same as autoregressive, and generation proceeds in fixed-size blocks (e.g., 512, 1000, 32) then continues autoregressively with a vanilla logits prediction head for length. Text diffusion today is discrete diffusion (tokens in, tokens out), though latent-space variants exist in literature. Low-latency diffusion suits on-device applications (robotics, phones) where batch sizes are small; quality matches frontier models and the bottleneck is serving throughput, not quality. RL can be applied with algorithmic changes. Combining diffusion with autoregressive models is possible. Initializing from a smaller model's output instead of noise adds training complexity since the model expects noise. Windows are set in stone and not revisited.
